title: JPMorgan Chase CEO says he's not running for president but 'never say never'
description: ABC News Chief Business Correspondent Rebecca Jarvis speaks with Jamie Dimon, CEO of JPMorgan Chase, 10 years after the financial crisis, on "This Week."

asr.full_text: And now to our exclusive interview with CEO Jamie Dimon, the head of JPMorgan Chase. He is one of the last remaining bank CEO's who worked through the 2008 financial crisis, which began with the collapse of Lehman Brothers ten years ago this weekend. Now, a decade later, could a Wall Street executive like Dimon be the next businessman to make a run for the White House? Our Rebecca Jarvis caught up with him, this week in New York. Why not throw your hat in the ring, Jamie? I said this before Trump was elected. You're not gonna get a wealthy New Yorker elected president. I was dead wrong. And by the way, this wealthy New Yorker actually earned his money. It wasn't a... it wasn't a gift from Daddy. JPMorgan's CEO, Jamie Dimon, taking aim at the president, saying he could beat Donald Trump in a potential 2020 match-up. Because I'm as tough as he is. I'm smarter than he is. I... I would be fine. He could punch me all he wants. It wouldn't work with me. I'd fight right back. But immediately after, in our exclusive interview, Dimon back-pedaled. I shouldn't have in our exclusive interview, Dimon backpedaled. Yeah, I shouldn't have said it. And more out of frustration and the little my own machismo, but I shouldn't have said it. It also proves I wouldn't be a good politician. President Trump seemed to agree, firing back on Twitter the next morning. The problem with banker Jamie Dimon running for president is that he doesn't have the aptitude or smarts and is a poor public speaker and nervous mess. Otherwise, he is wonderful. Dimon, who once served on the president's now disbanded strategy and policy forum, says a run for the White House is out of the picture...for now. So, you're done with politics? Yes. No running for president for you? No. Ever? Well, I'd never say never to anything but no. But the Wall Street titan is wading into public policy, from immigration to health care, and yes, Donald Trump. Unemployment below 4%, the market is at record highs, and consumer confidence is booming. Yeah. How much credit does the president deserve? You know, when President Trump was elected, confidence skyrocketed. Consumer, small business, large corporate, and because pro-business, pro-competitive taxes, pro some regulatory reform, and that has helped the economy. So, it's impossible to be to tease out how much, but it has helped the economy. Just like President Obama helped to stop the economy getting much it's impossible for me to tease out how much. But it has helped the economy, just like President Obama helped to stop the economy from getting much worse. But they also did policies, I think, that slowed down growth. So, some of those are being reversed. So yeah, he should take some credit for that. What kind of grade would you give President Trump purely on the economy? I'd say pretty good. B plus? A minus? Yeah, something like that. Diamond is optimistic about the current economy. But ten years ago, it was a very different story. Financial institutions are in trouble. 158-year-old Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy. Stock giant Merrill Lynch was sold after just two days of discussions. It is all a bit dizzying. Are we in a place where the banking system will never see something like that happen again in the United States? Well, I think you're mistaken to say the banking system. The banking system is very, very, very healthy and regulators should actually take a little bit of victory lap because Lehman would not happen today, but there will be a recession one day, but it won't be the banking system. It'll probably be something else. Banks got a considerable amount of the help. Do you think they've done enough post-crisis to help rebuild this economy? So I think your question is a little unfair. All the banks... Banks got help. I mean, I think the government did the right thing. I want to give full credit. And TARP was a part of that. But not all the banks needed that. And all banks including J.P. Morgan continued to lend money every day to all their clients nonstop around the world. Also some cause the problem. I understand that the American public looks at it and is unfair and it was. They look at it like the elite Washington Washington banks, a bunch of stuff. Kind of got bailed out and they suffered and there's some truth to that and they didn't see Old Testament justice. So I understand why there's a lot of anger out there. How would you in your role resolve that anger? I can't. There's nothing I can do. All I can do is serve my client everywhere around the world. Do good things. Try to earn our respect every day with our clients and communities. That's the best I can do is serve my client everywhere around the world do good things try to earn our respect everyday with our clients and communities that's the best I can do and this week JPMorgan pledged to invest 500 million dollars in communities over the next five years through its advancing cities initiative we know that working with government working with civic society working with business how can you lift up affordable housing jobs education entrepreneurs of, entrepreneurs of color, and all these things that can make these cities better.
